slide1.description2: Like many children in Bangladesh, Rafi goes to school every day
slide1.description3: Today, we will follow Rafi and help protect his neighbourhood from cholera.

slide2.description1: Every day, Rafi goes to school from 8 am to 5 pm. At home and at school, he uses water from shared water sources for washing and consumption. When the water is clean (light blue), Rafi and his family stay healthy.

slide3.description1: One day, Rafi becomes infected with cholera (Rafi turns red). As Rafi is infected, he contaminates the water at school and at home (it turns dark blue). When Rafi's family drinks contaminated water at home, his whole household becomes infected (the house turns red).

slide4.description1: Rafi lives in a community with many neighbours. The children go to the same school and drink water from the same water source. Rafi and another student are infected with cholera, and contaminate the school water. The infected students then bring cholera back to their families. See how fast cholera spreads when more neighbours are infected.

slide5.description1: People who have cholera can develop symptoms such as severe diarrhoea, vomiting, thirst, fatigue, muscle cramps, and dizziness. If they feel unwell, they should choose to stay at home for 3 days to avoid spreading the infection.
slide5.description2: In our town, neighbours who stay at home are shown with a green border. See how isolation slows the spread in the community.

slide6.description1: Even when infections slow down in Rafi’s neighbourhood, people continue to move around - going to school, to work, and doing activities in other neighbourhoods. Cholera can spread to other neighbourhoods via infected people. Testing people quickly and encouraging isolation helps protect many communities, not just Rafi’s.

slide7.description1: Thank you for helping protect Rafi’s community.
slide7.description2: Everyone’s movements matter! Isolating when you have cholera symptoms can prevent outbreaks and save lives.
slide7.acknowledgement-text: This work was developed by Hilman Prakoso at the Mobility Science Lab, University of Leeds, in collaboration with the Stevens Group, University of Oxford, as part of the ‘Integrated Surveillance Suite for Targeting Interventions to Cholera Outbreaks’ project, funded by the Wellcome Trust.
